strengths: Novel application of scale-wise ("next-scale prediction") autoregressive modeling to fMRI-to-image reconstruction, offering a genuine alternative paradigm to the dominant diffusion-based pipelines in this subfield.

The Hierarchy-to-Hierarchy Alignment scheme, which pairs fMRI encoder blocks to specific CLIP layers via cascaded MSE + SoftCLIP losses, is a reasonable and well-motivated design that is empirically validated via ablations (Table 2, Table 3).
Strong efficiency gains (4.67x faster inference than MindEye2) are convincingly demonstrated and are a practically meaningful contribution.

Comprehensive ablation studies isolate the effects of hierarchical features, CLIP layer mapping strategy, and coarse-to-fine vs. inverted guidance ordering, providing good support for the design choices.

Additional analyses (brain grounding/localization task, pycortex voxel-prediction visualization linking model blocks to visual cortex hierarchy, cross-subject and low-data results in appendix) add depth and partially support the paper's cognitive-alignment narrative.
The determinism/consistency advantage over stochastic diffusion baselines is clearly illustrated (Fig. 4) and is a meaningful practical property for reproducible neuroscience decoding.
Pseudo-code and implementation details are provided, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Low-level fidelity results are mixed: in the non-auxiliary-feature setting, MindHier underperforms several baselines on some metrics (e.g., SSIM 0.381 vs. Takagi et al. 0.410; AlexNet(2) 94.0% vs. Wills Aligner 95.8%), yet the paper's narrative emphasizes only the metrics where it wins (high-level semantic ones), giving an imbalanced framing of results.

The two-table structure (with vs. without auxiliary low-level feature) makes direct, fair comparison across all baselines and MindHier somewhat confusing, and MindHier's headline gains are concentrated in high-level/semantic metrics rather than a uniform improvement.

Key ablation studies (Tables 2-4) are conducted only on a single subject (Subject 1), limiting confidence that the observed design-choice effects generalize across subjects with different data quality/noise characteristics.
Standard deviations are reported for MindHier but not for baseline methods, making it difficult to assess whether reported improvements are statistically significant.

The core technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (VAR/Switti backbone, layer-wise CLIP distillation, cross-attention conditioning) adapted to a new domain, rather than a fundamentally new modeling technique; novelty is more architectural/application-level than conceptual.

No comparison against some recent hierarchical/multi-level fMRI decoding methods explicitly mentioned in related work (e.g., NeuroPictor, which also claims multi-level modulation), leaving open whether the proposed hierarchy is uniquely effective versus other multi-level schemes.
The paper does not discuss or analyze failure cases, nor does it include any human/perceptual evaluation despite strong claims of "high-fidelity" and cognitively-aligned reconstruction.

The deterministic nature of the model, framed purely as an advantage, is not discussed with respect to its potential downside of reduced diversity/uncertainty representation compared to stochastic generative approaches, which could be relevant given the inherent ambiguity of decoding from fMRI.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reformulation of fMRI-to-image reconstruction as a coarse-to-fine, scale-wise autoregressive problem, moving away from the dominant diffusion paradigm and addressing a clearly articulated limitation (fixed, single-level neural guidance) of prior work.

The Hierarchy-to-Hierarchy Alignment scheme (cascaded MSE loss + SoftCLIP loss) is a principled way to disentangle multi-level fMRI representations and is grounded in known ViT layer-wise behavior (Raghu et al.).

Strong empirical results: SOTA or near-SOTA on high-level semantic metrics (CLIP, Inception, SwAV, Eff) with a substantial 4.67x inference speedup and much lower variance/higher reproducibility than diffusion baselines.

Comprehensive diagnostic experiments (impact of hierarchical features, CLIP layer mapping strategy, coarse-to-fine vs. inverted guidance) provide reasonably convincing evidence for each design choice.

Additional analyses (per-subject results, low-data/single-session training, brain-region interpretability via voxel encoding, brain-grounding via Shikra localization, cross-subject qualitative consistency) considerably strengthen the empirical case and connect the method to neuroscience.
Good reproducibility support: detailed implementation section, pseudo-code for key algorithms, and stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: Low-level fidelity metrics (PixCorr, SSIM) are not consistently state-of-the-art; without the auxiliary low-level feature, MindHier underperforms methods like Wills Aligner (PixCorr) and Takagi et al. (SSIM), indicating the coarse-to-fine autoregressive approach trades off some structural/pixel fidelity for semantic fidelity.

Diagnostic/ablation experiments are conducted only on a single subject (Subject 1), which limits confidence that the observed trends (e.g., layer-mapping choice, coarse-to-fine ordering) generalize across subjects with different data quality/noise characteristics.

Several recently published, relevant baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., NeuroPictor, MindTuner, BrainGuard) are omitted from the main quantitative comparison table, leaving the completeness of the SOTA claim somewhat uncertain.

Evaluation is restricted to a single dataset (NSD); no cross-dataset or out-of-distribution evaluation is provided to assess generalizability of the hierarchical alignment and scale-aware guidance strategy.

Inference procedure selects the best of 4 generated candidates via CLIP similarity, which is standard practice in prior work but the paper does not clearly verify whether all compared baselines use an identical candidate-selection protocol, raising a minor concern about fair comparison.
The framework builds heavily on an existing pretrained VAR backbone (Switti) and mainly contributes the conditioning/alignment mechanism; the underlying generative backbone novelty is limited.

Claims connecting the method to cognitive neuroscience principles (e.g., Navon's "forest before trees") are somewhat anecdotal/qualitative rather than rigorously validated against behavioral or neural benchmarks beyond the voxel-encoding visualization.
